recent_posts.title: Security-driven Rapid Release - Pwn2Own Documentary (Part 4)
recent_posts.summary: A documentary-style account of Mozilla's response to a Firefox zero-day exploit demonstrated at Pwn2Own Berlin by Manfred Paul. The exploit targeted a JIT bounds-check elimination bug in the linear sums optimization, allowing out-of-bounds array access via integer underflow. Mozilla's team received the exploit details in the disclosure room, analyzed why existing fuzzers (particularly Fuzzilli) missed the 4-year-old bug — likely due to Spectre mitigations and debug build performance differences. Within hours, a patch was developed (an early return disabling the optimization), reviewed, and shipped as Firefox 138.0.4 in under 12 hours — a potential new record for Mozilla's 'chemspill' security-driven rapid release process. The piece also explains browser sandbox mechanics and why Pwn2Own renderer-only exploits disable the sandbox via MOZ_DISABLE_CONTENT_SANDBOX.

recent_posts.title: Firefox JIT Bug - Pwn2Own Documentary (Part 3)
recent_posts.summary: A documentary-style deep dive into Pwn2Own Berlin 2025, following security researcher Manfred Paul as he exploits a JIT bounds check elimination bug in Firefox. The bug involves a wrong optimization in the TryEliminateBoundsCheck function where 32-bit integer overflow semantics are ignored after the bitwise OR-with-0 trick is optimized away, allowing out-of-bounds memory access. Manfred explains his manual code review approach (no fuzzing), his mathematical background as an asset, and how he identified the conceptual flaw. The exploit successfully achieves remote code execution by browsing to a web page, earning $50,000 at the competition. Mozilla engineers are shown receiving the disclosure and beginning their rapid patch process.

recent_posts.title: The First Exploit  - Pwn2Own Documentary (Part 2)
recent_posts.summary: A documentary-style account of Mozilla's response to a Firefox zero-day exploit demonstrated at Pwn2Own Berlin. Researchers from Palo Alto Networks exploited an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in SpiderMonkey's implementation of Promise.allSettled. The piece follows Mozilla engineers Freddy and decoder through the disclosure room, back to the Mozilla office, and through their incident response process — including bug reproduction, bisection, patch development, and coordination with downstream users like Tor Browser. It also explores the nuances of patching open-source software where landing a commit can signal a security fix to adversaries, and why Mozilla chose to wait for day two exploits before pushing a release.

recent_posts.title: Inside Pwn2Own Berlin how Mozilla handles live Firefox zero-day exploits
recent_posts.summary: A documentary-style account of Pwn2Own Berlin, the world's most prestigious hacking competition, told from the perspective of both attackers and defenders. The story follows two Firefox zero-day exploits: researchers from Palo Alto Networks and returning champion Manfred Paul target Firefox, while Mozilla's security team treats the event as a live fire drill to practice incident response. The video covers the competition's structure, the $50,000 exploit trade, and Mozilla's internal process for analyzing and patching vulnerabilities within 90 days.

recent_posts.title: From Zero to Zero Day (and beyond) - Life of a Hacker: Jonathan Jacobi
recent_posts.summary: Jonathan Jacobi is a young cybersecurity professional with an impressive career trajectory. At just 24, he's a successful CTF player and founding member of Perfect Blue and Preston. He worked as a vulnerability researcher at Checkpoint and Microsoft and served in the military. Currently, he is part of the CTO team at the cybersecurity startup Dash IO. Jonathan's journey highlights the importance of seizing opportunities, leveraging networks, and persistently pursuing interests in cybersecurity.

recent_posts.title: The German Hacking Championship
recent_posts.summary: German students participate in the Deutsche Hacking Meisterschaft (German Hacking Championship), competing in CTF challenges to showcase their hacking skills. The event builds networking opportunities and relationships among participants, fostering potential career paths. Sponsored CTF challenges create unique and engaging experiences, such as ATM hacking. Former participants have gone on to have successful careers and even form their own companies. The event is seen as a significant opportunity for young people interested in cybersecurity.

recent_posts.title: Identifying Go vulnerabilities through blackbox testing
recent_posts.summary: Security audits for web applications can reveal backend implementations through error messages, stack traces, and other hints. A particular focus is on the Go language and its libraries, which can introduce specific vulnerabilities. The post discusses a challenge involving Go's concurrency features, highlighting a race condition vulnerability. Understanding these nuances can optimize testing and ensure more thorough security evaluations, especially when having access to the source code.

recent_posts.title: Google's Mobile VRP Behind the Scenes with Kristoffer Blasiak (Hextree Podcast Ep.1)
recent_posts.summary: Kristoffer Blasiak from Google, responsible for the Mobile VRP, discusses the process and challenges of handling Android application vulnerabilities. The conversation covers the reporting process, the importance of proof of concept, common types of vulnerabilities such as intent redirections and permission issues, and the scope of Google’s Mobile VRP. The podcast highlights the need for clear and detailed bug reports and the significance of Android security education.

recent_posts.title: My theory on how the webp 0day was discovered #short
recent_posts.summary: A theory explaining how a 0-day vulnerability in the webp image format might have been discovered, focusing on the trust in the output of a tool called enough.c to calculate maximum table sizes. The theory suggests that other image formats or compression tools that rely on similar assumptions might also be vulnerable.

recent_posts.title: My theory on how the webp 0day was discovered (BLASTPASS)
recent_posts.summary: A discussion on the webp 0day vulnerability known as BLASTPASS, exploring how this type of exploit might be discovered by targeting messaging services like iMessage. The author theorizes that the vulnerability in image parsing code was identified through extensive research and fuzzing, highlighting the complexity and effort involved in such advanced security research. The post emphasizes the importance of image file formats as a common source of security issues and details how researchers could have potentially found this vulnerability by examining similarities across different image parsers.
